The basal metabolic rate of Gemsbok, Oryx gazella, reflects its adaptation to arid, thermally challenging environments. Respirometry trials conducted at a mean core body temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C] have established a maximum oxygen consumption of 43,560 milliliters per hour [JOi = 43,560 milliliters per hour]. This elevated metabolic output, calculated from an adult body mass of roughly 180,000 grams [Wwi = 180,000 grams] for males, underscores the significant energetic costs associated with thermoregulation and maintenance in a large-bodied bovid inhabiting hot, water-limited landscapes. The species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate size, with males attaining a significantly greater body mass than females. Records indicate that the ultimate wet weight of females typically stabilizes around 190,000 grams [Wwi = around 190,000 grams], whereas males commonly reach an ultimate wet weight of 220,000 grams [Wwi = 220,000 grams], a disparity that likely reflects divergent selective pressures on male body size for intrasexual competition.

Reproductive output in Gemsbok is relatively modest, consistent with the life-history strategy of a large, long-lived ungulate. Under the stable thermal conditions of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], females typically produce a single calf per parturition event [N_R_i = single calf per parturition event], and the maximum number of successful birth events recorded annually is approximately 1.3 per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.3 per year]. This low reproductive frequency is characteristic of species that invest heavily in each offspring, a pattern further reflected in the considerable amount of time devoted to gestation and early maternal care. The gestation period extends for 270 days [tg = 270 days], a duration that is relatively protracted compared to some other antelope species of similar body mass and one that facilitates the development of a highly precocial neonate capable of keeping pace with the mobile herd shortly after birth at a temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C]. The maximum daily reproduction rate is expressed as 1.3 per year [Ri = 1.3 per year].

Neonatal Gemsbok enter the world at a substantial size that contributes to their immediate survival. Field data consistently report a wet weight at birth of 12,000 grams [Wwb = 12,000 grams], a mass that equips the calf with sufficient energy reserves to withstand periods of maternal absence during the first few days of life. The mother-offspring bond is intense during the early suckling phase, but weaning into nutritional independence occurs relatively early given the size of the calf. Under the thermal regime of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], calves attain a wet weight at weaning of approximately 35,000 grams [Wwx = approximately 35,000 grams] and typically complete their transition to a fully herbivorous diet at 77 days after birth [tx = 77 days after birth]. This weaning age is relatively brief when compared to other large bovids, likely an adaptation allowing the mother to regain body condition and resume cycling in the short seasonal window of resource availability.

The developmental trajectory from birth to reproductive maturity is governed by a combination of nutritional access and environmental conditions. At the typical metabolic temperature of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 550 days after birth [tp = 550 days after birth], a milestone that corresponds roughly to 1.5 years of age. This means that individuals are capable of participating in the breeding herd well before they have attained their full adult body mass, a pattern seen in other large ungulates that occupy unpredictable environments where early reproduction can offset the risk of extended periods of drought-related mortality. The attainment of sexual maturity at this age is further supported by observations of young males beginning to show interest in estrous females and young females experiencing their first ovulatory cycles.

The maximum lifespan of Gemsbok under free-ranging conditions has been documented at 23.8 years [am = 23.8 years], with this longevity recorded in individuals maintaining core temperatures of 38.9 °C [T = 38.9 °C]. This figure is comparable to that of other similar-sized desert-adapted antelope and reflects the species' relatively slow pace of life, characterized by low reproductive output and a long period of potential reproductive activity. Given the harshness of their native environment, where water and forage can be unpredictable, the ability to persist for over two decades provides multiple opportunities for successful breeding across a lifetime, buffering against years of poor recruitment. Older animals often exhibit worn dentition and reduced body condition, yet they continue to contribute to herd dynamics through social experience and the maintenance of stable dominance hierarchies.
